title.source: How can an artwork help us understand a society?

essentialQuestion.source: How can an artwork help us understand a society?

learningGoal.source: Tell what you can see in an artwork from what its history explains, describe its composition and medium, and explain why an artwork gives a chosen view of people's lives.

evidence.question.source: Edo-period Japan, around 1830–32, and Antwerp in the southern Low Countries, 1565. Look at the whole of each work first, then at its details.

read.sections.0.heading.source: Images have makers, audiences and settings

read.sections.0.text.source:
Art history studies images and objects together with the people who made, supported, bought, and used them. An artwork's composition, or arrangement, directs attention. Its medium, or material, affects how it was made and how people experience it. Two different works connect artistic choices with work, wealth, and the ways people picture their surroundings.

Katsushika Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830–32, during Japan's Edo period. It belongs to a series called Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. Curving water fills the picture, while the mountain appears as a small triangle in the distance. His landscapes used indigo and imported Prussian blue, so an image of a Japanese place also connects with materials that moved across borders.

Edo-period Japan was governed by the Tokugawa military government. Growing cities and trade supported prosperous merchants and craftspeople, often called chōnin, or townspeople. Their spending helped keep a market going for pictures of actors, entertainment, and famous places. Money did not give merchants the highest official social rank. Buyers' interests mattered alongside artists' ideas and government rules. Hokusai worked within this city culture; his prints do not express everything about Japan.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art history looks at objects and the people around them. Who made them? Who paid? Who used them? The composition is how the parts are arranged. It leads your eye. The medium is what a work is made of.

Hokusai made Under the Wave off Kanagawa around 1830 in Japan. Huge waves fill the picture. Mount Fuji is a small shape far away. He used a blue paint that came from Europe. So a picture of Japan also used things from far away.

At that time, military rulers governed Japan. Cities grew. Many traders and craftspeople had money. People called them townspeople. They bought pictures of actors and famous places. But money did not give them the top rank. Hokusai made prints for this city market.

read.sections.1.heading.source: How a woodblock print was made

read.sections.1.text.source:
This work is a woodblock print. A design is transferred to a block of wood. Areas are cut away, and the raised surface takes the ink. Paper laid over it takes the image. Colour printing uses separate blocks lined up on the same sheet. Many impressions, or printed copies, can come from the blocks.

Several specialists worked together. The designer supplied the image, a carver prepared the blocks, a printer added the colours, and a publisher ran the business. Publishers helped choose subjects and how carefully a print was made. A famous artist's name identifies one contribution within a wider world of skilled work and business.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
This picture is a woodblock print. A design is put on a block of wood. Some parts are cut away. Ink goes on the raised parts. Paper on top takes the picture. Each colour has its own block. Many copies, called impressions, come from the same blocks.

Many people made one print. An artist drew it. A carver cut the blocks. A printer added the colours. A publisher sold the prints. So a famous name is only one part of the work.

read.sections.2.text.source:
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Harvesters is an oil painting on oak from 1565. Workers cut grain and rest beneath a tree. A wealthy merchant in Antwerp ordered its series of seasons for the dining room of his country house. The Metropolitan Museum of Art describes the farm scene as sympathetic, but idealised for that patron.

Here the word Netherlandish describes a historical region, not the Dutch state of today. Antwerp, now in Belgium, belonged to the Low Countries, ruled by the Habsburg family. It was a centre of trade, printing, and art markets. A picture of the countryside could hang in the cultured home of someone whose wealth and daily life were in the city. Knowing this setting stops us from mistaking the patron's chosen view for the life of every farm worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers; a commissioned painting served one patron and one room. Both organise attention, but their audiences and ways of making differ. Form and historical context together help explain how each work belonged to a society.

read.sections.2.simpler.source:
Bruegel painted The Harvesters in 1565 on a wooden panel. Workers cut grain and rest under a tree. A rich trader in the city of Antwerp was its patron. He paid for it. It hung in the dining room of his country house. The museum says the scene is kind to the workers. But it is nicer than real life.

Antwerp is now in Belgium. Then it was a busy city of trade and art. So this picture of farm work hung in a rich city home. It shows his view, not the life of every worker.

A print was made in many copies for many buyers. A painting was made for one person and one room. Looking at the work and its context together helps us understand it.

read.glossary.0.definition.source: How the parts of an artwork are arranged.

read.glossary.0.example.source: In Hokusai's print, the composition puts the wave in front and the mountain far away.

read.glossary.1.definition.source: The material or materials an artwork is made with.

read.glossary.1.example.source: The medium of The Harvesters is oil paint on a wooden panel.

read.glossary.2.definition.source: One printed copy made from a printing block.

read.glossary.2.example.source: Museums around the world own impressions of the same print.

read.glossary.3.definition.source: A person or group who pays for or orders an artwork.

read.glossary.3.example.source: The patron of The Harvesters was a rich merchant.

read.glossary.4.definition.source: The time, place and people that help explain a work.

read.glossary.4.example.source: Knowing the context tells us who bought Hokusai's prints.

write.prompt.source: Pick Hokusai's print or Bruegel's painting. Explain how one thing you can see and one fact from its history help you understand it. Two or three sentences are enough.

write.sentenceStarters.0.source: In the picture, I can see ...

write.example.source: In Hokusai's print, I can see a huge wave in front and Mount Fuji very small behind it. The history tells us that prints like this were made in many copies and sold to townspeople in Japan's growing cities. Together, these show that the picture was made to catch the eye of buyers. It does not show everything about life in Japan.

speak.partnerTask.source: With a partner, describe how a print and a painting can be different kinds of historical evidence. Think about how many copies were made and who they were made for.

speak.independentTask.source: Say or type a short explanation of how a print and a painting can be different kinds of historical evidence.

educatorNotes.0.source: The two works give chosen views of life, not photographs or complete surveys. Keep what learners can see apart from what the history explains, and don't treat visual features as a secret code with one meaning.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a learner names something they can see (the arrangement, a material) and a supported fact about how the work was made, who paid for it, or where it was used. Accept different well-reasoned connections; simple English is fine.

educatorNotes.2.source: This is an approach adapted from art history, not a copy of a museum lesson. A learner can learn the whole explanation without doing any extra looking tasks.

educatorNotes.3.source: Edo-period context comes from The Met's essay Art of the Pleasure Quarters and the Ukiyo-e Style (2004), used only for Tokugawa rule, the city market and the gap between merchants' wealth and their formal status. Antwerp's art market and Bruegel's patrons come from The Met's timeline of the Low Countries and Jacob Wisse's essay on Bruegel.

educatorNotes.4.source: Many impressions of Hokusai's print exist in different museums. The image and the accession number here are The Met's impression, JP1847; don't attach another museum's number to this image.
